new_statements.quote: [...] Vowel length is phonemic, as evidenced by the difference in pronunciation between the following [...] short vowels appearing in longer forms and long vowels in shorter (preferably monosyllabic) forms, as [...] (sometimes heard as ga:ji). Syllabic stress is not phonemic. 1.5 In word-final position, whether in words of more than one syllable [...]
new_statements.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1971. Notes on the Bandjalang dialect spoken at Coraki and Bungawalbin Creek, N.S.W. (Australian Aboriginal Studies 32, Linguistic Series 11). Canberra: Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies.
new_statements.locator: Part I 'Speech Sounds' (pp. 1-2 per the table of contents; 'Structure of the Word' begins p. 3), the numbered paragraph on vowel length immediately preceding §1.5 (§1.3 or §1.4); exact printed page not recoverable from the snippets (p. 1 or 2)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer states only that syllabic (word) stress is non-phonemic, i.e. not contrastive, in the Coraki/Bungawalbin Bandjalang dialect, while vowel length is phonemic; he gives no rule for where stress falls. (Sharpe 1997:372, for the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain including Lower Richmond, implies default first-syllable stress with a long vowel elsewhere attracting the perceived stress; Holmer 1983 §2.9, for his Queensland survey languages only, notes a tendency to stress the second syllable of long words.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in Holmer 1971. Holmer 1983 (Queensland languages, not this one) mentions secondary stress on alternate syllables after the second.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Holmer 1971. Sharpe 1997:372 (pan-dialect): stress falls on other than the first syllable when that syllable has a long vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Syllabic stress'); the only other use of 'stressed' in the book is a sentence-level remark that clitic particles follow 'a stressed word toward the beginning of the sentence'. Data = 1964 field notes from two speakers (EF: Coraki/Bungawalbin; BT), i.e. citation and text forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lowe1444 'Lower Richmond' = Sharpe's Lower Richmond group (Nyangbal, Wiyabal, Coraki Bandjalang, Galibal); dialects in Glottolog: Bandjalang [band1358] (Coraki/Bungawalbin, Sharpe's 'Wuyebal'/BJ), Wiyabal [wiya1239] (Lismore), Njangbal [njan1241] (Ballina/Cabbage Tree Island). Holmer 1971 describes the Coraki/Bungawalbin speech of Mrs Evelyn Ferguson (EF) plus a second speaker (BT); Holmer 1983 calls it 'the Lismore and Bungawalbin Bandjalang', so the statement covers band1358 (and possibly wiya1239). The Sharpe 1997 stress remark is for the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain, and Crowley 1978 / StressTyp2 / WALS 'Bandjalang' statements are for Waalubal [waal1238] of Middle Clarence [midd1357], not this language.

sources.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1997. Dialect differences in Yugambeh-Bundjalung. In Tryon & Walsh (eds), Boundary rider: essays in honour of Geoffrey O'Grady, 365-391. Pacific Linguistics C-136. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p.372 (text lines 447-449), said of Watson's diacritics but stated for the whole dialect chain: 'An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.' p.373: 'where the stress patterns of the language force a vowel shortening'. Defines Lower Richmond = Nyangbal, Wiyabal, Coraki Bandjalang, Galibal (p.~370, line 362) and uses Holmer 1971 as the Wiyabal/Wuyebal (Lismore/Coraki) source (WI/BJ).

sources.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Part I 2.9: 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length'; Manandjali 9.6: 'Stress is - as in all Australian languages studied by the present author - not distinctive.' Queensland languages only; refers to Holmer 1971 as 'the Lismore and Bungawalbin Bandjalang' (10.24) but gives no stress statement for it.
